# The Value of Innocence in Girls.

---

->Believe me, girls! to our lives<-
->Only innocence can give dignity,<-
->For a beautiful face<-
->Does not provide the heart's goodness.<-

->The roses of your cheeks wither,<-
->Like violets, like carnations;<-
->Only even with a pale face,<-
->The value of innocence does not wither.<-

->Alas — how many a girl without virtue<-
->Withers in her youth,<-
->When a beautiful face<-
->Does not correspond to her heart.<-

->In outward polish <note>original: "Bildung." While this usually means education, in this context it refers to external social refinement or "cultivated" appearances.</note> lies a lie,<-
->Virtue alone ennobles one’s features:<-
->One can only truly be beautiful to the noble<-
->Through the cultivation of the soul <note>original: "Seelenbildung." A key concept in 18th-century thought, referring to the internal moral and aesthetic development of a person's character.</note>.<-

## Warning against Lust.

---

To resist the lure of lust—
Youth, if you love happiness and life,
Let this be your daily wisdom.
Flee from flattering desire;
It robs you of your heart's ornament, <note>original: "des Herzens Zierde." In the moral language of the time, this refers to one's inner purity, honor, or virtue.</note>
And its joys turn into pain.

So as not to increase its nourishment,
Never let food and drink weigh down your heart
And be a friend to sobriety.
To conquer yourself,
Frequently deny yourself even permitted pleasures,
And steer your sensuality. <note>The text suggests that "sensuality" (Sinnlichkeit) is like a ship or a horse that must be steered or controlled by the will.</note>

Do not let your eye command you;
And to prevent lust,
Always be modest regarding your own body.
Flee the bold jokes of the shallow wit, <note>original: "Witzling." A derogatory term for someone who thinks they are clever but lacks true wisdom or moral depth.</note>
And seek example, true wit, and pastime
In the company of noble hearts.

**Vocabulary:**
Lust/Sensuality, Youth, Wisdom, Desire, Sobriety, Sensuality, Modest, Shallow wit, Pastime

<summary>This page contains a moral poem warning young people to resist sensual temptations through sobriety, self-denial, and the avoidance of crude company. It emphasizes that true wisdom lies in controlling one's desires to preserve the "ornament of the heart."</summary>

<keywords>morality, temperance, lust, virtue, youth, self-discipline, 18th-century ethics, modesty</keywords>

Man, when lazy toward diligence and work,
Falls upon the paths of idleness
Easily into the villain’s nest.
The shield of innocence is occupation. <note>original: "Geschäfte." While it can mean "business," here it refers more broadly to staying busy or having a useful purpose to occupy the mind.</note>
Withdraw from lust its power
By the sweat of your brow. <note>original: "Im Schweiße deines Angesichts." A direct reference to the biblical decree in Genesis 3:19, framing hard work as a moral necessity.</note>

Should its urge awaken to battle you,
Then wake yourself, to stifle it early,
Before it denies you your freedom.
To smother it at the very birth
Is easy; but hard it is to suppress
Once your heart has nourished it.

Often the urges of vice clothe themselves
In the form of permitted love,
And you do not perceive the danger.
Long acquaintance makes you more familiar; <note>original: "freier." Literally "freer," but in this social context, it implies a dangerous lack of formal restraint or being "too comfortable" with someone.</note>
And often a forbidden fire grows
From that which was friendship at the start.

Your feeling heart will forgive itself;
It will dread the eruption of vice,
Even as it nourishes its own urge.
You will believe yourself strong and secure,
And permit yourself small failings,
Until your virtue is dishonored.

**Vocabulary:** Diligence, Work, Idleness, Innocence, Lust/Sensuality, Freedom, Vice, Love, Friendship, Virtue

<summary>This page concludes a moral poem by arguing that hard work is the best defense against temptation and warning that vice often hides behind the guise of innocent friendship. It cautions that moral decay begins with small, self-excused failings that eventually destroy one's virtue.</summary>

<keywords>diligence, idleness, temptation, friendship, virtue, vice, morality, work ethic</keywords>

But no, you shall not dishonor them, <note>Likely referring to the objects of one's affection or the "permitted" friendships mentioned on the previous page.</note>
You shall always deny yourself the deed;
Is your heart therefore already virtuous?
Is it only sin to commit the act?
Should you not also conquer the urge,
Not also the desire of passion?

It is desires that shame us;
And without even completing them,
We already violate our duty.
If you do not blush <note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, the ability to blush was seen as a physical proof of a "pure" and "virtuous" soul that still felt shame.</note> before them,
If you do not kill the lusts through the spirit;
Then do not boast of your chastity! <term>Keuschheit: Traditionally, the virtue of refraining from "impure" thoughts and actions, considered essential for moral character.</term>

Fill yourself, if you seem to waver,
Often with the powerful thought:
Innocence is the soul's happiness.
Once squandered and given up,
It leaves you for your whole life,
And no repentance brings it back.

Think often to yourself: The bonds of lust <note>original: "Wollust." In this moralistic context, it refers to sinful or excessive carnal desire rather than just "pleasure."</note>
Are not only a shame to the conscience,
They are also a mockery before the world.
And even if I could in darkness
Hide away the abomination of lust:
Yet God sees and finds me.

## On the Happiness of Marital Love.

---

What would our life be without love,
Which the Creator himself poured into our hearts?
Without it, our happiness would not be great,
If its beautiful impulses <note>original: "schönen Triebe." In this context, "Triebe" refers to natural, God-given inclinations or movements of the soul toward affection, rather than base instincts.</note>
Did not beat within us, did not guide us,
And did not spread joy and bliss <note>original: "Seligkeit." This term carries a dual meaning of intense earthly happiness and spiritual or eternal blessedness.</note> around us.

Yes, the Creator of our life saw this;
He weighed our happiness just as he did our hardship <note>original: "Ungemach." Refers to the various troubles, discomforts, or adversities of human existence.</note>.

## Noble Example of Gratitude.

---

During the reign of Louis XIV, King of France, Algiers was bombarded by a French fleet, and the inhabitants were greatly terrified. The launching of bombs caused great damage to the people of Algiers, and everyone was in extreme mortal danger. Because of this, they became so embittered toward the enemy that they fired all French prisoners back toward the fleet using cannons. <note>This refers to the 1683 naval bombardment of Algiers; historical accounts state the Algerian ruler used the French consul and other prisoners as "human cannonballs" in retaliation.</note> Among those unfortunate victims of rage and cruelty was a French ship captain. He too was led away, bound, and was just about to be fired off when a Turk standing nearby recognized him.

Formerly, this Turk had been a prisoner of the captain; he had been treated very kindly by him and finally set free again. The worshipper of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomets." A common historical European spelling of the Prophet's name, here used to denote the man's Islamic faith.</note> remembered this kindness he had enjoyed with all the liveliness of his spirit, and immediately pleaded for mercy for

### The Faithful Wife.

---

Hidden beneath the cover of a thicket of hazel bushes, where the valley—winding its way into pleasant wildernesses <note>The German "Einöden" suggests a secluded, uninhabited area, often used in a Romantic sense to describe a place of peaceful solitude.</note>—withdrew from the eye, there sat Alcindor <note>Alcindor is a name typical of the pastoral and sentimental literary style popular in the late 18th century.</note> deep in thought upon a fragment of rock. This stone had once been torn from the fearsome cliffs by a mighty hurricane and, during the hours of suffering nature <note>This poetic phrase refers to a violent storm or natural upheaval, personifying nature as being in labor or distress.</note>, was hurled down into the startled plain.

### Alcindor’s Love.

Their days flowed along, like winding brooks through flowery meadows. — O how Semine loved her husband, how Alcindor loved his wife. Years soon became fleeting days, and hours hurried away like minutes.

A contented smile drew Semine’s gaze to her husband’s brow. Alcindor adored her; with every passing day her sparkling eye grew darker <note>German: "schwärzte sich." In the aesthetic language of the time, "darkening" or "blackening" eyes often symbolized a deepening of soul, passion, or intellectual intensity.</note>, and her virtue <note>German: "Tugend." A core concept of 18th-century "Empfindsamkeit" (Sentimentalism), referring to a combination of moral purity, modesty, and emotional sensitivity.</note> gained new charms.

Seek insight <note>Erkenntniß: This term suggests both a rational understanding and a deeper spiritual realization, central to the Enlightenment ideal of self-improvement.</note> early, and prepare yourselves for a higher enjoyment.

## Letter to Amyntor.

---

My friend!

You, who were once so dear to my soul—how deeply has passion <note>Leidenschaft: In the 18th century, "passion" (passion) was often viewed as a dangerous, overwhelming emotion that overpowered reason and led to moral downfall.</note> dragged you down toward the abyss? I would not be your friend—would never have deserved your love—if I were to remain silent at the very moment when you are so close to your ruin <note>Verderben: This term implies moral or spiritual perdition, suggesting that the friend’s current path is leading to a state of total destruction.</note>. —

# True Contentment.

---

Contentment, you are the desire of the
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;entire world,
Yet by the greatest part, the path 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;to you is missed.
One seeks you, but how? One seeks, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;after the manner of the blind,
Not where you are, no! But there, where one 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;wishes to find you.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The great <note>meaning the nobility or those in high positions of power.</note> seek you in high rank, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;state, and splendor,
And in the expansion of their 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;countries' power;
They look out discontentedly from their golden
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;thrones
Upon the too-small number of millions 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of servants.
Their own possessions displease their 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;dulled senses:
Therefore their arm reaches for the sword, and 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;demands more gain.

## To Cidalise. <note>The name Cidalise was a common literary pseudonym in 18th-century "gallant" literature, often used in moralizing letters or poems addressed to women.</note>

---

You complain, dear friend! that your husband has withdrawn his love from you, and you accuse him of infidelity. I do not defend him, dear Cidalise! when I tell you that in human life there is no happiness that is not mixed with melancholy <note>Original: "Wehmuth," a state of wistful sadness or yearning.</note>. You may be at peace, Cidalise! if it did not happen through your own fault; and be also content when I tell you that it lies within your power to lead your husband back again.

I do not defend your husband, Cidalise! often renouncing the heart of his wife. # The Mother
## to her Child in the Cradle.

---

Yes, destiny <note>Original: "Verhängniß." This tender name is so sacred to my heart, and its pronunciation sounds so movingly in my soul. What, indeed, is the brilliance of all grand titles compared to this tender name! O you, the sole object of my wishes, beloved child! How dear you are to my heart!

# To Sophie.

---

->Dear Wife!<-

After so many failed attempts that I have made to make you aware of yourself, and of the consequences of your behavior, I choose—in order to have at least done everything that lay within my power—this further path: to accuse you before your own self, and to call upon your otherwise so clear reason to be the <term>judge <note>Original: *Schiedsrichterinn*. The feminine form of "judge" or "arbitrator." The author is appealing to the Enlightenment ideal that "Reason" should be the ultimate authority in settling personal and moral disputes.</note></term> between the two of us. We have now been married for five years, Sophie! You know whether, in all this time, I have shown you the unchanged, always constant continuation of a tenderness that knew no bounds at its inception. It is not my place to boast of the <term>rights <note>Original: *Gerechtsame*. This refers to the moral prerogatives or "claims" the husband feels he has earned through his virtuous behavior toward her.</note></term> over your heart that I have gained through the <term>anticipation <note>Original: *Zuvorkommenung*. A key concept in 18th-century "Sensibility," referring to the act of fulfilling a loved one's needs or wishes before they are even expressed.</note></term> of your wishes, through my attentive respect, and through my tender devotion.

Sophie! to neglect anything here, or to prefer our <term>inclinations <note>Original: *Neigungen*. Do not, for example, the satisfaction of your inclinations, your <term>finery <note>Original: *Putz*. ## Wish of a tender wife,

### as she handed her husband a
### flower.

---

Husband! <note>Original: *Gatte*. A formal but affectionate term for a spouse common in the 18th and 19th centuries.</note> take this flower—
It is now what I still am,
Blooming, young, and beautiful:
But it will also, just like me,
Believe me, husband! surely,
Soon fade away into nothing.

Think: your wife also blooms for you,
But she consecrates <note>Original: *weiht*. This implies a sacred dedication to a higher moral standard.</note> herself to virtue,
Should beauty flee;
So, when youth departs,
Which only resembles a flower,
Her heart will still continue to bloom.

## by von Berghofer. <note>Franz Xaver von Berghofer was a philosopher and writer of the late 18th and early 19th centuries who wrote extensively on family life and virtue.</note>

## On the Female Sex <note>Original: *Vom Frauenzimmer*. In the 18th century, this term was a polite way to refer to women collectively or the "female sex." By the 19th and 20th centuries, the word's meaning shifted to become a derogatory slang term, but here it carries its original, respectful meaning.</note>

---

The character of the women of our age <note>Original: *Zeitalter*. The author is likely writing during the late Enlightenment or the Age of Sensibility (late 1700s).</note> is so strange that one can find almost no term to express it. There were once times in which the marks of female goodness were easily identified! But now they are the most wavering, indistinct, and deceptive. Fashion, high society, affectation <note>Original: *Ziererey*. This refers to an over-refined, artificial manner of behaving or speaking intended to impress others.</note>, and affected sentimentalism <note>Original: *Empfindeley*. A pejorative term for "Sensibility" (*Empfindsamkeit*), suggesting that the emotions displayed are fake, exaggerated, or performative rather than sincere.</note> rob all those marks of inner goodness of heart and adopt false exteriors, which in the time of our ancestors no female art, no varnish of education <note>Original: *Erziehung*. This implies the social grooming and "polishing" young women received to fit into high society.</note>, and no expression of sympathy learned only in the "great world" <note>A common idiom for high society or fashionable circles.</note> knew how to imitate. How pleasant it must have been then, when one still beheld beauty and innocence on unpainted brows. — Angelic souls still shone from the undisguised eye of the girl, and

<summary>The author begins a critique of contemporary women, arguing that modern fashion and high-society manners have replaced genuine "goodness of heart" with artificial affectation and fake sentimentality. He contrasts the "unpainted" sincerity of past generations with the deceptive social performances of his own time.</summary>
<keywords>women, social critique, Age of Sensibility, affectation, fashion, morality, 18th-century society</keywords>

# Conversation.

---

**Limane.** But sister! You really should have more respect for the public <note>original: *Publikum*; in the 18th century, this refers to "the world" or high society whose opinion governed a person's standing.</note>. Half the world believes that Raymund is your husband. You are always seen with him. — Sister! You surely owe some reverence to common reputation <note>original: *gemeinen Ruf*; referring to the public rumor or one's general standing in the eyes of others.</note>. —

**Philinde.** Raymund is my friend. I owe him many obligations <note>original: *Verbindungen*; this can refer to social debts, favors, or the bonds of friendship, though here it implies a relationship that borders on the improper.</note>.

**Timant.** Oh yes! But is your husband any less your friend? Do you have fewer obligations toward him?

**Philinde.** I know quite well what I owe him.

# A Boy’s Wishes
## on his father’s name day.

->A domestic scene.<-

---

**Boy.** Yes, dearest father! — It is really so! — My heart tells me so. —

**Father.** What does it tell you, dear boy? —

**Boy.** That what I spoke were only wishes, — that wishes mostly remain what they are, — and that it is painful to feel things that one is unable to do. — This thought makes me restless; it mingles the joys of today with sadness. <note>In the 18th century, "sensibility" or "Empfindsamkeit" was a popular literary movement that emphasized deep, often melancholy emotions as a sign of a virtuous character.</note>

A cold shudder flows through every one of my limbs:
my steps falter, and a ghastly fear
takes hold of my heart.
But why does my foot tremble on the path
where it glides?
Why does sweat drip from my brow?
Am I not here — here, where the end of all
misery lies? —
Away with you, you images of terror! —
Tyrants created you. <note>original: *Tirannen*; the author suggests that the terrifying, demonic depictions of death were invented by "tyrants" (secular or religious) to keep the living in a state of fearful submission.</note> — Death smiles kindly,

Come! give me your hand, final companion of mortals! —
and receive from me the gratitude of the sufferer,
whom you lead with kindness out of the prison of this life. <note>original: *Kerker dieses Lebens*; a common 18th-century metaphor where the soul is seen as being liberated from the "jail" of the physical body and earthly suffering.</note>
Your gaze already seems lovelier to me,
your eye already gentler. —
Why then should I tremble before you?

# A n e c d o t e.

---

A gallant woman <note>original: "galante Frau"; in the 18th century, this referred to a sophisticated woman of the world who engaged in refined social and romantic maneuvering.</note> desires to be truly loved. For a coquette <note>original: "Kokette"; a woman who trifles with men's affections to feed her own vanity.</note>, however, it is enough if she is merely considered amiable and beautiful. The former seeks to make conquests; the latter, however, is satisfied with pleasing. The first goes from one understanding <note>original: "Verständniß"; in this context, a romantic arrangement or a secret mutual agreement between lovers.</note> to another; the second, however, creates many kinds of pastimes for herself at once. With the one, passion and pleasure prevail; and with the other, vanity and frivolousness. Gallantry is a weakness of the heart, or perhaps a natural flaw; coquetry, on the other hand, is a disorder of the mind <note>original: "Verstand"; meaning the intellect or rational faculty.</note>. The gallant woman makes herself fearsome; the coquette makes herself hated. If one combines these two characters, one will find a third, who is the worst
un-

## Letter from a Wife

### to her frivolous husband.

---

With a heart full of a love, of which perhaps no one but I can truly conceive <note>original: "einen Begriff hat"; literally "has a concept of," implying a depth of feeling beyond common understanding.</note>, and with an anxiety for your well-being that is equal to this tenderness, I venture to write to you about a matter of which I would not have the heart to speak with you in person. ...the character of the one who is to govern this family, guide the conduct of the mistress of the house <note>original: "Hausmutter"; in the 18th century, this term referred to the female head of a large household, emphasizing her role as a provider and manager rather than just a spouse.</note>, rule the domestic servants <note>original: "Gesinde"; the collective term for the staff, including maids and farmhands, who lived within the household.</note>, educate the children, and provide for the well-being of them all? — Can these duties, my beloved *Lindor!*; can their performance and their valuation coexist with an unrestrained, frivolous, or dissolute life?

Believe me, there is no middle ground <note>original: "Mittelstraße"; refers to a neutral path. The author argues that a head of household cannot be morally "neutral"—he is either a force for good or a source of corruption.</note> here, and this is chiefly because everyone follows his example—becoming infected by his vices, or at the very least suffering and perishing under his disorders. For will not, for example, the wife of a man who has surrendered himself to drink, to gambling, or to any other disorderly passion, be in danger? If she is endowed by God with only a weak, soft soul and fragile intellectual faculties, and if her virtue is not raised above every temptation, will she not be in danger of being delivered over to some similar, punishable passion—or perhaps one even worse and more shameful? This might happen through the feeling of the injustice done to her, through the grief over the neglect she suffers, and over the misfortune befalling her entire house. And will not then the unhappy children—who are then without support, without a guide to lead them toward the good and [fill] them with...

# Evening.

### Translated from the English.

---

She flees, the smiling goddess of the day <note>original: "Göttin des Tages"; likely a personification of the sun or the dawn, such as Aurora or Hemera</note>, she flees unwillingly away from the earth occupied with folly, and willingly and gladly leaves the stage to her more modest brother <note>The personification of Evening or the Moon; in German, the word for evening (Abend) is masculine</note>, who kindly hides many scenes of nonsense under the covering veil of coming darkness. Now he reigns on earth—every day’s work is finished. Mild coolness, soothing silence, and the darkness that strengthens the eye <note>It was a common historical belief that the soft light of evening "strengthened" or healed eyes strained by the harsh glare of the sun</note>, hover over exhausted nature, pouring out new streams of life for the future day’s work over her. These benefits of the night are fair and just—they are the earned reward of weary nature for the duties assigned and performed by the Creator. But man!—and I, among men—My day too is finished; also

to me, the milder evening and the beneficial night grant their refreshing blessings unasked. But does not active nature put my lazy idleness to shame? Does her holy obedience to the laws of her Creator not expose the disobedience of my sins? How much has been neglected! How many things have gone unthought! And how much more did my pious intentions resolve to do—intentions that were hindered by corrupt passion and turned into nothing by lazy sluggishness—

Ha! How is it that man is so weary, so faint, so easily exhausted when it comes to doing good, and yet so lively, so active, so strong, so busy with foolishness, with trifles <note>original: "Spielwerken"; literally "play-works," referring to frivolous distractions or unimportant gadgets</note>—or, oh the shame of it—even with vices! It is as if evil paid higher wages than virtue, or as if its influence were more powerful than that of piety. Yet—do we fools not know this?—it keeps ruin waiting in ambush, rewards only with punishment, and its influence is more poisonous than the plague <note>original: "Pestilenz"; a common historical reference to the Black Death or infectious disease as a metaphor for moral corruption</note>. And yet—as the day flees, so life flees. Nothing is done that ought to be done, and there is no master we serve more faithfully than sin. Virtue

### The Language of the World and the Language of Religion, when Slander Grieves your Soul.

---

World. **R**evenge yourself! said Wrath. — He has wounded your honor; he has stained your good name; he has cast his own vices upon you: Revenge yourself! You have the opportunity to hurt him deeply: you can do it easily, you can do it without harm <note>That is, without risk of retaliation or legal consequence to oneself.</note> to yourself. —

Religion. No! answered Gentleness <note>original: "Sanftmuth," a key 18th-century virtue meaning a mild, patient, and humble disposition, often translated as "meekness" in biblical contexts.</note>. You shared so many pleasures with him; he received so many kindnesses from you.

World. All the worse! Would you let the ungrateful one go like that?

I have often reflected on how, given their pride, they can content themselves with such a meager portion of the sciences <term>Wissenschaften: in the 18th century, this referred to all systematic branches of knowledge, including the humanities and philosophy</term> for their own persons. And perhaps I have discovered the reason. Here, my friends, is my conjecture!

A certain writer compared the sciences to strong drinks, of which no one should consume more than his head can withstand. Perhaps our young freethinkers <term>Freigeister: a term for skeptics who rejected traditional religious dogmas, often used pejoratively here to imply superficiality</term> have read this, and—out of an all-too-modest mistrust in the strength of their own heads (which, after all, does not otherwise seem to be their failing)—have carried sobriety too far. To be sure, if I may be permitted to say so, I can perceive traces of such mistrust in them just as little regarding wine itself as on many other occasions; yet all men often possess great inconsistencies in their characters.

Wissenschaften <gloss>Sciences/Knowledge</gloss>, Stolz <gloss>Pride</gloss>, Freigeister <gloss>Freethinkers</gloss>, Mistrauen <gloss>Mistrust</gloss>, Nüchternheit <gloss>Sobriety</gloss>, Charakteren <gloss>Characters</gloss>

## The Commandment of the Lord:
## You shall not steal.

->Preliminary introduction regarding the de-<-
->sire of mankind for temporal<-
->goods.<-

Swap the persons in your thoughts. Be the one he is, and let him be the one you are. Let his circumstances, fates, needs, means, and so forth be yours, and in your mind, lend him what belongs to you. This will teach you immediately whether your need or his is greater. For the equal lack of one and the same thing does not yet constitute an equal need.

**Extravagance** consists of the thoughtlessness of preferring unnecessary expenses to those that are more necessary. # Greed acts in opposition to the Commandment

->Thou shalt not steal.<-

---

The vice most strongly opposed to this commandment is **<term>greed (Geiz)</term>** <note>The German word "Geiz" can mean both greed and stinginess, implying an irrational attachment to wealth for its own sake rather than its use.</note>, one of the most ridiculous and irrational of all **<term>passions (Leidenschaften)</term>**, because it is based merely on a hollow opinion without relating to any real object.

All other passions seem to provide a sense of pleasure to those who are possessed by them. They flatter the senses, and their seed is planted in **<term>nature (Natur)</term>**. Although they bring many evils in their wake if one indulges in them to excess, they are ev-

--- Page 299 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 280, completing the thought that while natural passions may be accompanied by pleasure, the vice of greed (Geiz) is inherently miserable. It picks up from the partial word "ev-" on the previous page, completing "ever."</meta>

ever accompanied by pleasure. By contrast, **<term>greed (Geiz)</term>** <note>In this context, greed refers specifically to the hoarding of wealth (stinginess) rather than just the desire for more.</note> in and of itself brings torment to the fools who surrender to it, and never appears as anything other than shrouded in dark worries.

What **<term>folly (Thorheit)</term>** is it not, to collect things in abundance that have no value apart from their use, only to make no use of them? To cling to the possession of a thing that is merely a representing sign <note>The author refers to money/currency as a "sign" of value rather than the value itself.</note>, without ever wishing to obtain what it represents; to constantly embrace an empty shadow while simultaneously and stubbornly driving away the real object?

This **<term>vice (Laster)</term>** always causes a dark mood, whereas **<term>nature (Natur)</term>** arouses only happy and pleasant **<term>passions (Leidenschaften)</term>**. The **<term>miser (Geizhals)</term>** is neither man, nor father, nor friend, citizen, or human being; he is nothing at all but a—miser.

...than the one who is ruled by envy. All other vices occupy themselves with objects that are, to a certain degree, good, or that deserve to be feared, hated, and detested to a certain degree. ...that he makes them his ultimate goal <term>ultimate goal (Endzweck): the final purpose or highest aim toward which one's actions are directed.</term>, or hopes to obtain them through actions that make him unworthy of a better approval—and that is all too often merely the ambiguous or vain praise of the crowd. --- Page 308 ---
<meta>This page (290) continues the analysis of envy from page 289, moving from a definition of the vice to a comparison with other "passions" such as greed and ambition, highlighting why envy is uniquely devoid of social value.</meta>

How shameful a vice envy is becomes further evident from the fact that other excessive passions <term>passions (Leidenschaften): in 18th-century philosophy, these were powerful emotional drives that often competed with reason.</term> can coexist with certain external perfections—which, while fundamentally not moral, nonetheless *appear* to be so—and can even drive one to strive for them. Envy, by contrast, completely stifles the desire to be good (or at least to appear good) in any way, because it presupposes a sense of despair or a total discouragement <note>original: "Muthlosigkeit"</note> regarding the possibility of surpassing others. 

The sensualist, the ambitious man, even the greedy and the vengeful can possess civic virtues <term>civic virtues (bürgerliche Tugenden): social behaviors that benefit the community or state, regardless of whether the person's internal motives are pure.</term> that have no small influence on the general happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit," a central term in Enlightenment ethics referring to flourishing and well-being.</note> of this present life, even if they contribute nothing to their own true welfare. The sensualist can be obliging, helpful, and pleasant in social company; the ambitious man can undertake great and brilliant deeds; there are greedy men who do not deceive so that they themselves might not be deceived; and the vengeful man is not an enemy to his fellow human beings until he has been insulted—

### True benevolence is the opposite of envy.

---

My active desire to increase the well-being of my fellow creatures is benevolence <term>benevolence (Gutherzigkeit): In Enlightenment philosophy, this "good-heartedness" was seen as a rational virtue—a "thätiges Verlangen" (active desire) that required action, distinguishing it from mere passive sympathy.</term>. In this way, it distinguishes itself from any ineffective goodwill, from every surging, soft-hearted impulse, and from the emotions of pity, which can only relate to the unfortunate. The good heart expresses itself toward enemies, toward the happy and the unhappy, toward those of high and low status. For one and the same reason, I feed the hungry, clothe the naked, tend to the wounded man who had fallen among murderers <note>This is a direct reference to the Parable of the Good Samaritan from the New Testament (Luke 10:30), emphasizing that benevolence extends even to strangers or social outcasts.</note>, rescue the slandered reputation of my offender, increase the joys of the happy, lighten the slave’s chain, and ease the pains of the sick and sorrowful; for one and the same reason, I take pi— <note>original: "erbarm'". This is a catchword, the beginning of the word "erbarmen" (to take pity/have mercy), placed at the bottom of the page to show what the first word of the next page will be.</note>

...[idlers] to feed, who naturally prefer such a life to earning their daily bread through labor.

The truly <term>good-hearted person (Gutherzige): Someone possessing "Gutherzigkeit," an Enlightenment-era term for innate benevolence or a "good heart."</term> can only have the well-being <note>original: "Wohlstand"; in this context, it refers to the general welfare and moral health of a person, not just financial wealth.</note> of another as their aim. If, therefore, he is likely to know that his charitable acts would actually worsen the other’s condition, it is evident to him that he must set limits to his good will in this matter. To do otherwise would be to risk falling into a <term>folly (Thorheit): A lack of moral wisdom or practical judgment.</term> that is ruinous to both himself and others. 

The excuse—"I am doing good; what does it matter to me how it is used? My intention, after all, is to help the other person. Is it my fault if I do not achieve it? I gave to one who required my support; whether he was worthy or unworthy of my gift, I did not know and was not meant to know"—can only be valid in cases where it is either a matter of a mere trifle, or where pressing circumstances demand immediate assistance if help is to be rendered at all.

...because he believes that his good deeds should speak for him; or a fear of people, to which his temperament already has a natural inclination, holds him back from **self-defense**; or an exaggerated **modesty** drives him to wait for a more convenient time, when he might put it into effect with less violation of the strictest **rules of etiquette**. Blessings and rewards of every kind, such as beautiful souls <term>beautiful souls: original "schöne Seelen"; an Enlightenment-era ideal describing an individual whose natural inclinations are perfectly in harmony with their moral duties</term> desire, will follow closely in your footsteps! You will be the object of the respect of your fellow citizens and the respect of your own heart; and an example for every good youth who comes after you and hears of your name!

<summary>The author warns that a wasted youth cannot be recovered even with tears and exhorts young men to pursue wisdom, virtue, and learning to earn the respect of society and their own conscience.</summary>

And when you then look back upon the days gone by and convince yourself that they are irretrievable, how the blessed awareness will swell your heart <note>original: "deine Brust erweitern"; literally "expand your breast," a common 18th-century idiom for a feeling of profound emotional satisfaction or moral pride</note> that although they are gone from you forever, they are not irretrievably lost to you. — — What can the idle man be thinking when he chooses to be active not today, but only tomorrow! If he does not wish to act because he is *unable* to do so, then he need not excuse himself; but if he is able to act and yet refuses, then he shall find no excuse for himself anywhere. The man who possesses the power to act does so with that very strength as soon as he can, if he wishes to be a man of noble character; for he is animated by a burning zeal <note>original: "Eifer"; in this context, it refers to a passionate, virtuous drive toward one's duties</note> to perform his good deed, and he feels no satisfaction with himself until the deed stands before him as a completed task. Should he, if he can attain this self-satisfaction today, not wish to partake of it this very day? Furthermore, he must not place too much trust in his own powers. Perhaps tomorrow he will no longer possess them in all their fullness as he does today.

The more I reflect on the similarity of my days to these waves <note>original: "Fluthen"; literally "floods" or "tides," here used metaphorically to represent the flowing, unstoppable passage of time</note>, the more sacred the duty becomes to me to employ them in the most worthy manner. ### Just is the grief when we mourn the noble one who leaves us in death. <note>Original: "Billig ist der Schmerz." In this 18th-century context, "billig" does not mean "cheap" but "just," "equitable," or "fitting."</note>

---

No pains are more just and more human than those which we feel at the death of our loved ones; <note>Original: "der Unsrigen," literally "our own," referring to family, kin, and close-knit circles.</note> whether they are united with us through nature and through all the connections which spring from that source, or even only through their character, through the similarity between us and them, through their companionship, and through the manifold ties of a tender and intimate friendship, and according to the judgment of our affection, are indispensable to our present happiness. Our soul loses, through the separation from them, even if it fear- <note>The word is broken across the page: "befürch-" likely completes as "befürchtet" (fears or feared).</note>

feared—the enjoyment of its noblest and most pleasant joys. ...I [know] how great the pain is that separation from them causes, especially when it strikes us suddenly and unexpectedly; and when does it ever strike us if not unexpectedly and while we are unprepared? Therefore, I always suffer alongside those who are brought into such a sensitive trial, even those who face it with composure and steadfastness—but most of all with those among them who have a special claim to my esteem and love. Even my advanced years have so little power over my melancholy <note>Original: "Wehmuth." the days of your being together! <note>original: "Beisammenseyns"</note> A promise from God that you should remain together on earth forever in this way would have been, for you, a promise of heaven brought down to earth and fulfilled.

This promise, dear ones, was not granted to you. You would have been worthy of it; however, the universal, original destiny of mankind <term>Menschenbestimmung: a central Enlightenment concept regarding the inherent purpose and ultimate fate of human beings</term> did not permit it. While we are together, we may enjoy to the fullest extent the happiness that loving hearts grant one another. God himself assists us in this. In such moments, He already perceives in us a faint image of what we shall be to one another when the fear of death <note>original: "Todesfurcht"</note> no longer hovers around us. But when the hour strikes that separates lovers—then the first promise <note>original: "Verheissung"</note> has reached its end for them.

Lucinda! Therefore, noble souls, so long as they live united, should enjoy the bliss of their fellowship <note>original: "Gemeinschaft"</note> with a heartfelt urgency.

But, why did *Alphonso*, that most tender husband, sink away from his even more tender wife so early? Is it not enough that lovers are not granted eternities to love upon this earth? ## Hilarius’s Contemplation of Death.

---

Writing, for me, means speaking with many all at once—revealing to them the innermost depths of my soul—my empathy <note>The original "Theilnehmung" implies a deep, active participation in the feelings of others, a core value of the 18th-century Cult of Sensibility.</note>—telling them that a creature lives who seeks other creatures in return. To speak is a necessity of the heart—sentiment flows from heart to heart, feeling from soul to soul.

O all of you, who are dear to my heart—fellow humans and brothers! grant me your love, just as my heart is entirely your own. —

If I can be of use to any one of you through any of my powers, which God or nature gave me—then come, dear creature! and grant me the pleasure of the most sublime feeling: to be a human and a brother. —

If I cannot help, then have compassion for me, and do not despise the sympathetic tear that flows from my eye for you. — Hand in hand, let us then look toward Heaven—to Him, who is the Savior of mankind.
